newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria president vetoes foreign investment law.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria president vetoes foreign investment law.

text.p: Bulgaria's President Zhelyu Zhelev on Wednesday vetoed new amendments to the foreign investment law, saying they would deter new investment and were contrary to the national interest.

"(The amendments) not only fail to create a more favourable investment climate, they scrap some of the current benefits and impose new barriers to foreign investment," state news agency BTA quoted Zhelev as saying in a letter to parliament.

On November 28, parliament approved amendments introducing a minimum $50,000 foreign investment registration threshold, denying profit repatriation and other investment incentives to some 6,800 smaller joint-venture companies.
The director of Bulgaria's foreign investment agency, Daniela Bobeva, resigned after the Socialist-dominated parliament approved the amendments.
"This amendment virtually denies protection to all small investors which are the majority of foreign investors in Bulgaria at the moment," Zhelev said.
Similar limits might be appropriate for countries which face a huge inflow of investments but they were inadequate for Bulgaria, which badly needs foreign investment, Zhelev said.

Supporters of the amendments say they extended some tax benefits in a bid to speed up privatisation, exempting non-fiscal foreign investments like machines and equipment, patent rights, licences, trademarks, technologies and know-how from Value Added Tax, customs duties and other taxes.

The president criticised an amendment which set a 10-year limit after registration in Bulgaria for protection of foreign investments against possible legislative curbs that might come into force during that period.
Until now, foreign investors could rely on this preferential legislative treatment indefinitely.

The president also criticised the amendment banning foreign investors from farmland ownership irrespective of their stake in a joint venture. So far the ban applied only for foreign investors holding more than 50 percent stake.
"Instead of revising and possibly easing the curbs new ones were introduced, which will continue to repel foreign investments," Zhelev said.
An amendment denying preferential treatment for foreign investors with double citizenship was also attacked by the president.

"People who had left Bulgaria in the last decades for political and economic reasons and now have chosen to make investments because of their links to the country, will have to give up their Bulgarian citizenship or will be turned away because of this amendment," said Zhelev.
Parliament is dominated by the Bulgarian Socialist Party, while Zhelev is supported by the anti-communist opposition Union of Democratic Forces.
The bill will now be returned to parliament, where the Socialists have a majority. Opposition parliamentary groups could appeal to the constitutional court as a last resort.

Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment among its ex-communist neighbours. The Balkan country of 8.4 million people has attracted around $800 million in investments from abroad since 1990.
